# tools-handin

The hand_in tool: a task session hands its finished work in and stops.

- **Runs in:** the harness process
- **Source:** [lisp/modules/harness-tools-handin.el](../../lisp/modules/harness-tools-handin.el)
- **Loaded:** when enabled (see `harness-enable-modules`)
- **Requires:** [tools](tools.md), [session](session.md)

## About

A task session that is sure its work is done says so with `hand_in`
instead of just stopping: the tool records the final summary and the
evidence for it, and ends the turn as if the model had finished --
the review step then puts the task in front of the user as usual
(`agent/turn-ended` with `end-turn`).  It is the reverse of plan
mode: where `plan` stops before the work to agree on it, `hand_in`
stops after it to hand it over.

The problem statement is required too, and an optional reproduction
note: a short summary of what must be fixed and how to see it, which
the review shows at the top, so the user remembers what a task was
about when its name alone does not say.  The resolved report rides
the tool result's `:meta`, so the transcript can draw the same review
after the task left review.

Evidence is required, and at least one item; the tool description
tells the model that an image or a video is required whenever the
work has anything to show, and that a claim about a command (the
tests pass) belongs there as a reference to the tool call that made
it.  A call is named by its call id, its node id, the name of its
tool, or the `#N` handle the error on a miss lists -- the model
never sees its own call ids, so the name and handle make the common
case work on the first try.  Referenced calls are copied into the
report as a snapshot -- title, input, output, error flag -- so the
task view can show them as the link they are without re-reading the
session, and the file keeps them.

The tool also takes two optional flags.  `cannot_continue` is for a
task that cannot be finished: it goes to the user's input instead of
review, nothing merges, evidence may be empty, and the refusal while
a sub-agent's merge is pending does not apply.  `no_merge` is for
work that needs no merge -- an informational task, or one that
changed nothing -- and verifying it completes it without the merge
queue.

The tool is offered to task sessions only: the filter `agent/tools`
removes it where there is no task to hand the work in to.

## Provides

### Tools

- `hand_in` — Hand the finished work in and stop: the turn ends and the task waits for the user's review, with your summary and evidence in front of them. Call it once, when you are sure the task is complete, instead of replying normally. problem is required: a short summary of what must be fixed and how to see it, which the review shows at the top, where the task's name alone would not remind the user what it was about. summary is your final message, in markdown. reproduction is optional: how to see the problem, or the steps to check the fix, for the review. If the task cannot be finished, call it with cannot_continue true and say what blocks it in summary: it goes to the user's input instead of review and nothing merges. If the work needs no merge -- an informational task, or one that changed nothing -- pass no_merge true: verifying it completes without merging. evidence is required and holds at least one item; an item is an object with exactly one of: image or video (a path to a file you made, such as a screenshot); file (a path); code (with language); note (markdown text); or tool_call (an earlier call of yours, which the user then sees as a link to that call in the session). Show, do not tell: when the work has anything to see -- a UI, a rendering, a chart, a layout, anything a screenshot can show -- an image, or a video for motion, is required, not just nice to have; take the screenshot with bash first. Quote the tool call that proves a claim (the tests pass, the command's output) as a tool_call item. A file, code or note is evidence only when nothing visual applies. caption says what the item shows. A tool_call may name the call by its tool's name (the newest call of that tool, e.g. "bash"), by `#N` or `<tool>#N` as an earlier hand_in error listed it (1 = newest), or by its call or node id.
